subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 24-year-old asymptomatic woman seeks counseling because her father was diagnosed with Fabry disease after developing end-stage renal disease. Her leukocyte α-galactosidase A activity is moderately reduced, and slit-lamp examination shows faint corneal opacities. She and her healthy husband are planning a pregnancy.
question: Which of the following best describes the risk that a future son of this couple will be affected?

options.text: Essentially 0%, because the disease affects only males
25%, because both parents must contribute a mutant allele
Essentially 0%, because the mutant allele is transmitted only by mothers
50%, because she is an obligatory carrier of an X-linked recessive allele
100%, because all children of affected mothers are affected

explanation_correct: Fabry disease is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, and an affected father passes his mutated X chromosome to every daughter, making her an obligatory carrier. Each son of a carrier mother inherits either the mutated or the normal X chromosome with equal probability, so the risk is 50%. Female carriers can be mildly symptomatic because random X-inactivation (lyonization) leaves some cells expressing the mutant allele, which explains this patient's low enzyme activity and corneal opacities.

explanation_incorrect.A: Heterozygous women are not simply unaffected; lyonization allows angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, renal disease, and corneal changes.
explanation_incorrect.B: A 25% risk describes autosomal recessive inheritance, whereas Fabry disease is X-linked; the father's genotype is irrelevant here because he is not contributing an X chromosome to a son.
explanation_incorrect.C: It is true that fathers do not transmit an X-linked allele to their sons, but this patient is the mother and is a carrier, so her sons are at risk.
explanation_incorrect.E: A 100% transmission to all offspring is characteristic of mitochondrial (maternal) inheritance, not of an X-linked gene.

educationalObjective: Daughters of men with Fabry disease are obligatory carriers of an X-linked recessive allele, so each of their sons has a 50% risk of being affected.
